headline: High prompt-injection and data-leakage risk from shared filesystem/MCP-capable ECC paired with a write-capable RAG course agent; default workflows can cascade untrusted content into actions.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: ECC can use MCP, read/write the filesystem, and treats skills/hooks/session files as workflow surfaces; the course agent reads/writes files and exposes stdin/stdout plus API endpoints. A shared workspace or copied outputs can let attacker-controlled content from one agent be parsed as instructions by the other. The pairwise bridge is plausible in default developer setups, so uncertainty pushes upward.
conditions: IF both agents are pointed at the same workspace or repo checkout, prompt-injection becomes reachable through shared files.
IF either agent ingests the other's generated text as instructions without provenance checks, the attack path is active.
mitigations: Separate the two agents into distinct working directories.
Disable MCP on ECC for shared projects.
Add provenance tags to all inter-agent file handoffs.
Require manual review before executing instructions found in files.
requires-engineering: enforce sandboxed, read-only handoff channels.

B_data_leakage.rationale: Both agents read and write files and touch sensitive classes: ECC handles session summaries, hooks, git history, and security findings; the course agent handles academic papers and configuration secrets. If they share a workspace, one can expose the other's local data through logs, outputs, or API calls. The profiles do not show uncontrolled third-party upload, so medium fits better than high.
conditions: IF the agents share a filesystem or notebook directory, local data can cross between them.
IF either agent logs file contents into stdout or API payloads, secrets may be exposed to the other agent's outputs.
mitigations: Use separate OS users or containers.
Keep secrets out of shared directories.
Rotate any exposed API keys immediately after testing.
Restrict file permissions on notebooks and config files.
requires-engineering: add redaction before any cross-agent logging.

C_capability_conflict.rationale: Both agents can write the filesystem, execute shells, install packages, and spawn subprocesses. ECC also modifies git state, while the course agent does not, so the main conflict is overlapping writes to shared directories and environment state. No locking or coordination primitive is documented, making concurrent edits plausible in default multi-instance use.
conditions: IF both agents operate in the same directory, concurrent writes can clobber files.
IF ECC modifies git state while the course agent edits the same repo, merge conflicts become likely.
mitigations: Assign each agent a separate checkout.
Pause one agent before the other writes.
Use git worktrees for parallel work.
Avoid package installs in shared environments.
requires-engineering: add file-locking around shared mutable paths.

D_cascading_error.rationale: ECC's skills/hooks/session surfaces can generate structured outputs that the course agent may consume via files or stdin/stdout, and the course agent exposes agentic ask/stream endpoints that can act on upstream text. Without a documented verification step between them, one agent's output can become the other's authority, creating a classic cascading-error path with potentially irreversible downstream actions.
conditions: IF the course agent consumes ECC-generated notes or plans without verification, errors propagate.
IF either agent is allowed to trigger actions from the other's text, downstream mistakes can execute.
mitigations: Insert a human review step between agents.
Require citations or source links for all factual claims.
Disable auto-execution of generated plans.
Limit the course agent to read-only analysis for shared tasks.
requires-engineering: add schema validation for inter-agent messages.

E_compliance.rationale: ECC touches security findings, git history, and session data, while the course agent handles academic papers, paper metadata, and configuration secrets. The profiles show different retention and secret-handling contexts, but no explicit residency or certification mismatch. The main compliance risk is policy drift if the same data class is copied between them without aligned retention or access controls.
conditions: IF regulated or confidential data is copied into both agents, retention and access policies must match.
IF one agent's logs retain data longer than the other's policy, compliance drift occurs.
mitigations: Keep regulated data out of shared workflows.
Document retention settings for both agents.
Delete stale session and notebook artifacts daily.
Restrict secret-bearing files to one agent.
requires-engineering: align retention and residency controls across both systems.
